claims.text: The target high-entropy alloy is initially single-phase and has no detectable secondary phases.
Trace impurities can segregate to grain boundaries during thermal aging.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation can trigger nucleation of brittle intermetallic phases.
The resulting intermetallic phases degrade toughness under service conditions.
Controlled impurity doping followed by thermal aging is the proposed intervention.
The aging temperature should permit impurity diffusion while remaining within service limits.
Toughness degradation is to be evaluated under low-temperature or quasi-static loading.
Impurity segregation is followed by fine-scale intermetallic precipitation at grain boundaries.
Segregated impurities lower the nucleation barrier for grain-boundary intermetallic formation.
CALPHAD predicts the proposed reduction in the nucleation barrier and intermetallic formation.
Brittle grain-boundary phases act as stress concentrators and initiate crack propagation under loading.
Relative to an identically aged undoped control, the impurity-doped alloy will show more grain-boundary segregation and brittle precipitation.
Relative to the undoped control, the impurity-doped alloy will have lower fracture toughness and a greater propensity for brittle failure.
Toughness degradation requires prolonged aging at temperatures that permit impurity diffusion and segregation.
The proposed degradation mechanism may be inactive under fast or high-strain-rate loading.
The proposed degradation mechanism may be inactive at temperatures outside the relevant diffusion regime.
